st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged task-level capabilities, human verification or workflow redesign. It instead reframes the issue around opening the legal-services market to nontraditional providers and governing them through empirical, entity-level, risk-based oversight. This is constructively relevant to the cluster’s governance and access-to-justice themes, but it advances a materially different regulatory proposition.

st.t: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broad framing by defining access to justice as meaningful access to solutions—not merely courts or cheaper legal services—and by documenting widespread unmet civil legal needs across income levels. Its list of Utah initiatives is contextual and does not establish their effectiveness or directly develop the cluster’s fair-resolution criterion.

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing by treating meaningful access to justice—not investment or market entry alone—as the reform’s objective. Although it predicts that market-based innovation will improve access, it presents the sandbox as a supervised, time-limited experiment whose continuation depends on later evaluation rather than claiming demonstrated consumer benefit.

At the end of that period, the Supreme Court  will carefully evaluate the program as a whole, including the Sandbox,  to determine if it should continue.

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: The Standing Order directly endorses conditional experimentation to address unmet civil legal need while controlling consumer risk. It establishes limited rule relaxation, mandatory authorization, risk assessment, supervision and eventual review; its access benefits are stated expectations rather than demonstrated pilot outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: 9 A regulatory sandbox is a policy tool through which a government or  regulatory body permits limited relaxation of applicable rules to facilitate the  development and testing of innovative business models, products, or services  by sandbox participants.

The objective of the application process is for the Innovation Office to  determine that the legal service proposed by the applicant furthers the  Regulatory Objective and does not present unacceptable levels of risk of  consumer harm.

kp.k: Justice-gap evidence motivates legal market reform
kp.d: The Court cites the 2021 World Justice Project ranking of the United States as 126th of 139 countries on affordable and accessible civil justice and last among thirty-seven high-income countries. It also cites Legal Services Corporation findings that 86 percent of civil legal problems reported by low-income Americans in 2016–17 received inadequate or no help, and an April 2020 Utah analysis finding 82 percent unmet legal needs among Utahns living at 200 percent or less of federal poverty guidelines. These are background findings attributed to external studies, not measured sandbox outcomes.
qs: As to that same  factor, out of the thirty-seven high-income countries, the United States  ranks dead last.
of the civil legal problems reported  by low-income Americans in [2016–17] received inadequate or no legal  help.

kp.k: Market opening is proposed to supplement volunteer-based responses
kp.d: The Court argues that existing access initiatives and volunteering cannot bridge the justice gap without far-reaching market-based reform permitting new providers, business models and service options. It expects innovation and market forces to improve access while protecting consumers; the order expresses this as the Court’s belief rather than a demonstrated result.
qs: what is needed is  market-based, far-reaching reform focused on opening the legal market  to new providers, business models, and service options.

The Supreme Court believes that the regulatory  reform set out in this Standing Order will shrink the access-to-justice  gap by fostering innovation and harnessing market forces, all while  protecting consumers of legal services from harm.

kp.k: Sandbox admits nonlawyer ownership and technology-delivered legal services
kp.d: The regulatory scope includes businesses practising law with nonlawyer economic interests, profit sharing or decision-making authority; for-profit and nonprofit entities delivering legal services through nonlawyer providers or technology; and entities seeking discrete professional-rule waivers. This establishes a route for nontraditional service delivery rather than reporting AI-specific capabilities or adoption results.
qs: any business entity that includes nonlawyers who have an  economic interest, including profit sharing, or decision-making  authority in the business and engages in the practice of law as  defined in Utah Supreme Court Rule 14-802;

an entity, for profit or nonprofit, using nonlawyer alternative  legal providers or technology platforms, tools, or applications to  provide legal services constituting the practice of law as defined  in Utah Supreme Court Rule 14-802;
an entity, for profit or nonprofit, seeking a discrete waiver of the  Rules of Professional Conduct to facilitate innovative legal  service delivery.

kp.k: Regulation targets entities, objectives and consumer risk
kp.d: The Innovation Office is directed to regulate organizations rather than individuals, articulate objectives and allocate regulatory resources using data-driven assessments of risk. Its stated objective combines quality, innovation, affordability and competition in support of access to justice.
qs: Entity regulation: the Office will regulate organizations rather than  individuals.
To ensure consumers have access to a well-developed, high-quality,  innovative, affordable, and competitive market for legal services.
Using risk-based regulation  enables the Innovation Office to better prioritize its resources and  manage risks in the Utah legal services market.

kp.k: Risk comparisons recognize consumers may otherwise receive no help
kp.d: The order requires comparison against available legal services rather than perfect lawyer representation. It directs empirically supported, proportionate intervention, with acceptable-risk thresholds considering both probability and magnitude of harm. Market-based regulatory incentives should encourage desired outcomes by increasing participant revenue or reducing costs.
qs: risk should not be evaluated as against an ideal of perfect legal representation  by a lawyer.
In many cases, that means no access to legal  representation or legal resources at all.
The phrase “empirically driven” means that the regulatory approach and  actions must be supported, whenever possible, by data from the legal services  market.
regulatory tactics should seek to align regulatory incentives with increased revenue or decreased costs  for market participants in order to encourage desired behavior or outcomes.

kp.k: Court authorization is conditional, limited and discretionary
kp.d: Entities within scope must apply to enter the sandbox. Proposed services must further the regulatory objective without unacceptable consumer-harm risk. The Supreme Court retains final authorization authority, and permission extends only to the approved services under the authorization order; continued operation depends on compliance and absence of material consumer harm.
qs: Authorized participants and services  are deemed authorized to practice law or offer legal services in Utah,  albeit on a limited and temporary basis, under Utah Supreme Court  Rule of Professional Practice 14-802.
Authorization is always contingent  upon timely compliance with the requirements imposed by the  Innovation Office and upon a showing that the entity is not causing  material consumer harm.

kp.k: General-market entry requires safety evidence and continuing oversight
kp.d: Sandbox exit is conditional on the Court deciding to allow exits and exercising its sole discretion in each case. A satisfactory compliance record and no material consumer harm may support licensure, but exit does not end regulation: license terms retain monitoring, reporting and enforcement obligations.
qs: If the Supreme Court decides to permit Sandbox participants to exit the  Sandbox, entities that are able to demonstrate that their legal services  are safe—i.e., that maintain a satisfactory record of compliance and do  not cause material consumer harm during their Sandbox term—may, at the Supreme Court’s sole discretion, be approved to exit the Sandbox
Exited entities will remain under the regulatory authority of the  Supreme Court through the Innovation Office

kp.k: Monitoring combines provider data, complaints and proactive testing
kp.d: The Office may adjust reporting requirements to provider performance and compliance, assess data at provider, sector and market levels, and use independent monitoring methods. All regulated providers must proactively report unforeseen risks or harms. Consumer complaints feed into the broader risk-assessment system; these are mandated mechanisms rather than findings about actual service quality.
qs: All regulated providers, whether in the Sandbox  or in the general market, have a proactive duty to report any unforeseen  risks or harms of which they become aware.
including but  not limited to market surveys, expert audits, anonymous testing,  product walkthroughs, and “secret shopper” tests.
The Innovation Office will develop a  process by which individual complaint information is fed into the larger data reporting system to contribute to the assessment of risk.

kp.k: Consumer protection does not promise elimination of harm
kp.d: The Court expressly accepts that some harm may occur without regulatory enforcement, while preserving traditional civil and applicable criminal remedies. Enforcement generally responds to evidence exceeding acceptable harm thresholds, but noncompliance and lack of responsiveness can also trigger action. Available mechanisms include education, increased reporting, fines, suspension and termination, with formal interventions subject to Committee and Court review.
qs: sometimes there may be no regulatory enforcement  action  even  though  some  consumers  may  experience  harm.
Enforcement will generally be triggered when the evidence of consumer  harm exceeds the applicable acceptable consumer harm threshold.
Enforcement can also be triggered by failure to comply with the  regulatory requirements imposed by the Innovation Office and for lack  of responsiveness.

kp.k: Lawyers retain professional duties within nontraditional providers
kp.d: Under the cited Utah Rule 5.4(B), participation as an owner, employee, contractor or business partner does not release lawyers from professional-conduct duties. The order separately prohibits disbarred lawyers from holding ownership interests greater than 10 percent in authorized entities and requires disclosures about specified disbarment and felony-history relationships for risk assessment; felony history is not stated as an automatic exclusion.
qs: lawyers engaging with the nontraditional  provision of legal services, as owners, employees, contractors, or  business partners with Sandbox participants or licensed providers are  required to uphold their duties as required by the Rules of Professional  Conduct.
disbarred lawyers are not  permitted to gain or hold an ownership interest of greater than 10 percent in any entity authorized to practice law under Rule 5.4B or this  Standing Order.

kp.k: Transparency supports public accountability and external research
kp.d: Applications and applicant identities are presumptively public, with protection for appropriately designated confidential business information. Court-approved researchers may receive aggregate anonymized data under data-sharing agreements. Monthly Court reporting and at least annual public reporting must cover participation, services, consumers served, available demographics, risk trends and complaints, creating an evaluation framework rather than supplying outcome evidence.
qs: Identities of applicants to the Sandbox and  the applications themselves are presumed to be public information.

Nothing, however, in this section limits the ability of the Innovation  Office to provide aggregate and anonymized data sets to Court  approved outside researchers, subject to a duly executed data sharing  agreement with the Court.
The reports to the Supreme Court must be monthly.

kp.k: Seven-year pilot makes permanent reform conditional on evaluation
kp.d: The amended order establishes a seven-year pilot from August 14, 2020, expiring unless expressly continued by the Supreme Court. The Court will evaluate whether and in what form the program continues. Participants in good standing presenting little apparent consumer risk may receive discretionary continuation; successfully exited entities may continue under the Office or a successor regulator.
qs: The Supreme Court establishes the Office of Legal Services Innovation,  the Legal Services Innovation Committee, and the Sandbox for a pilot  phase of seven years from the original effective date of this Standing  Order (August 14, 2020).
unless expressly authorized  by the Supreme Court, the program will expire at the conclusion of the  seven-year study period.
At the end of the pilot phase, the Supreme Court will determine if and  in what form the Innovation Office will continue.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The order makes no explicit AI-specific claim. The Utah Supreme Court predicts that regulatory reform allowing new providers, business models and technology-enabled legal services will improve access to justice while protecting consumers.
pts.d: The Court attributes the expected improvement to innovation and market forces, not specifically to AI. It argues that volunteering alone cannot bridge the justice gap and that opening the legal market is necessary. Technology platforms, tools and applications delivering services constituting the practice of law fall within the sandbox's scope, but the order does not identify AI systems or predict their productivity, quality, employment or pricing effects. These are broader regulatory-reform expectations rather than reported results of AI adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The Court cites unmet-need studies and access-to-justice rankings to establish the problem; it does not supply measured evidence that AI or the sandbox has reduced that problem.
pts.d: The background cites the 2021 World Justice Project ranking of the United States at 126th of 139 countries for affordable and accessible civil justice and last among 37 high-income countries. It cites the Legal Services Corporation's finding that 86 percent of low-income Americans' reported civil legal problems in 2016–17 received inadequate or no help; California findings of widespread civil legal problems and 85 percent receiving no or inadequate help; and an April 2020 Utah analysis finding 82 percent unmet legal needs among people at or below 200 percent of federal poverty guidelines. These figures support the diagnosis of unmet need, not a demonstrated causal effect of reform. The Court also invokes its experience with existing access initiatives. The order establishes prospective data collection, monitoring and evaluation rather than reporting sandbox outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reform is a seven-year pilot beginning August 14, 2020, with continued authorization contingent on compliance, consumer-harm assessment and Court discretion.
pts.d: The supplied amended order provides for a seven-year study period ending August 14, 2027, unless expressly continued. It does not set a numerical target or deadline for reducing the justice gap. Sandbox entry is limited and temporary; exit into the general market is discretionary and depends on a satisfactory compliance and safety record. Risk is assessed against consumers' actual alternatives, including no legal assistance, rather than ideal representation. The Court expressly qualifies its consumer-protection expectation by acknowledging that harm cannot be eliminated and may sometimes occur without regulatory enforcement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Intended beneficiaries are Utah consumers with unmet legal needs; affected providers include nonlawyer-owned businesses and entities delivering legal services through nonlawyers or technology.
pts.d: The Court frames the benefit as access to affordable, high-quality legal information, advice, resources and courts for Utahns across socioeconomic levels, with low-income unmet civil legal need central to its justification. Providers gain a potential authorized route to deliver otherwise impermissible services or use nontraditional structures, subject to entity-level monitoring, reporting and enforcement. The scope concerns entities practicing law, not software vendors merely selling tools. Lawyers participating as owners, employees, contractors or business partners remain bound by professional-conduct duties. The order makes no prediction about lawyer displacement or staffing changes.
